source.title: How Ordinary People Changed History

cards.title: History is mostly made by people nobody had heard of
cards.body:
We often tell history as the story of kings, presidents and generals. But look closely at the biggest changes of the last two centuries and you find seamstresses, students, farmers, shipyard workers and office clerks at the heart of them.

They had no armies and little money. What they had was a clear sense that something was wrong, a willingness to act, and, crucially, other people beside them.

This guide tells some of their stories: a bus passenger in Alabama, a woman who escaped slavery and went back, Indian villagers making salt, Kenyan women planting trees, Polish workers, crowds at a wall in Berlin, and South Africans who wore down apartheid. Then it draws out what they teach about courage, organising, persistence and the power of small acts.
cards.apply_it: Write down one thing in your community you wish were different, however small.

quiz.question: What did most of the people in this guide lack?
options: A clear sense of what was wrong
quiz.explanation: They were ordinary people without official power, yet they changed history by acting together on a clear sense of injustice.

cards.title: Rosa Parks was not just tired; she was a prepared activist
cards.body:
On 1 December 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks, a 42-year-old seamstress, refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger and was arrested.

The popular story says she was simply tired after work. The truth is more inspiring. Parks had served for years as secretary of the local NAACP branch, investigating attacks on Black residents. That summer she had attended a workshop on organising for civil rights. She later made clear that what she was tired of was giving in.

She was also not the first. A teenager named Claudette Colvin had refused months earlier. What made Parks's arrest a turning point was that a network of people was ready to act. Courage matters most when it meets preparation.
cards.apply_it: Learn one fact today about a local cause you care about, so you are ready if the moment comes.

quiz.question: What does the real story of Rosa Parks show?
options: She acted on a sudden whim
She was the only person ever to refuse
Her courage was backed by years of activism and preparation
quiz.explanation: Parks was an experienced activist, and her stand worked because organisers were ready to turn it into a movement.

cards.title: The Montgomery bus boycott won because thousands organised for a year
cards.body:
Within hours of Parks's arrest, Jo Ann Robinson, a college teacher, and the Women's Political Council stayed up through the night printing tens of thousands of leaflets calling for a one-day boycott of the buses.

The one day became 381. Black residents, who made up most of the riders, walked miles to work, shared cars and used a carefully planned network of volunteer drivers and pick-up points. Churches raised money. A young pastor, Martin Luther King Jr., was chosen to lead the effort.

The city fought back with arrests and threats, and King's house was bombed. But the riders held firm, and in late 1956 the US Supreme Court upheld a ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional.

One brave act lit the spark. Patient, unglamorous organising kept the fire going.
cards.apply_it: Offer one practical form of help, such as a lift, a meal or an hour of time, to a cause or neighbour.

quiz.question: How long did the Montgomery bus boycott last?
quiz.explanation: Planned as a one-day protest, the boycott lasted 381 days, sustained by carpools, churches and volunteer organisers.

cards.title: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery, then kept going back for others
cards.body:
Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland. In 1849, fearing she would be sold, she escaped north on foot, guided by the North Star and by people along the Underground Railroad.

Many would have stopped there. Tubman returned about thirteen times over roughly a decade, leading family members and friends to freedom and giving directions to dozens more. Each trip risked capture and re-enslavement.

During the American Civil War she worked as a scout, spy and nurse for the Union Army. In June 1863 she helped guide a raid along the Combahee River in South Carolina that freed more than 700 enslaved people.

Tubman shows that personal freedom can become a starting point rather than an ending. Once you are safe, you can help others find their way.
cards.apply_it: Think of one way you have been helped in life, and pass a similar help on to someone else this week.

quiz.question: What did Harriet Tubman do after escaping slavery in 1849?
options: Returned about thirteen times to lead others to freedom
quiz.explanation: Tubman went back into danger again and again, and later helped lead a Civil War raid that freed more than 700 people.

cards.title: Winning the vote for women took decades of stubborn effort
cards.body:
In Britain, women campaigned for the vote from the 1860s onwards. The largest group, the suffragists led by Millicent Fawcett, used petitions, meetings and peaceful lobbying. In 1903 Emmeline Pankhurst founded a more militant group whose members became known as suffragettes. They heckled politicians, chained themselves to railings, smashed windows and, later, set fires. Many were jailed, went on hunger strike and were force-fed.

Historians still debate which tactics helped most. What is clear is that the pressure never let up. In 1918 some women over 30 won the vote, and in 1928 women gained the vote on equal terms with men. In the United States, the 19th Amendment came in 1920, after more than seventy years of campaigning.

Big change can take a lifetime. Keep going anyway.
cards.apply_it: Register to vote, or check your registration, and put the next election date in your calendar.

quiz.question: When did women in Britain win the vote on equal terms with men?
quiz.explanation: Some women over 30 gained the vote in 1918, but equal voting rights with men only came in 1928.

cards.title: The Salt March turned a pinch of salt into a challenge to an empire
cards.body:
In 1930, British rule in India made it illegal for Indians to make or sell their own salt, and taxed it heavily. Salt was something everyone needed, rich or poor, so the law touched every household.

Mohandas Gandhi chose it as his target. On 12 March he set out from his ashram with 78 followers and walked about 240 miles to the sea at Dandi. Crowds gathered in every village. On 6 April he picked up a handful of salty mud, breaking the law.

Across India, ordinary people copied him, making salt, boycotting British cloth and refusing to cooperate. Around 60,000 were arrested. At one salt works, unarmed marchers were beaten but did not hit back, and reports shocked the world. Independence came in 1947, built on many such acts.
cards.apply_it: Pick one everyday choice, such as what you buy, and align it with a value you care about.

quiz.question: Why did Gandhi choose salt as the focus of his 1930 protest?
options: Salt was a luxury only the rich used
It was a simple necessity every Indian household relied on
Salt was easy to sell abroad
The British had banned eating salt
quiz.explanation: Because everyone needed salt, the unfair law touched every household and was easy for millions to defy.

cards.title: Wangari Maathai started a movement with a single tree seedling
cards.body:
In 1977 Wangari Maathai, a Kenyan scientist and the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, began encouraging rural women to plant trees. Forests were being cut down, streams were drying up, and women were walking further every year for firewood and water.

Her Green Belt Movement paid women a small sum for each seedling that survived. Over the following decades it planted tens of millions of trees across Kenya and inspired similar work in other countries. Along the way, women gained income, confidence and a voice in public life.

Maathai was beaten and jailed for opposing corrupt land deals, but kept going. In 2004 she became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, honoured for linking the environment, democracy and peace.
cards.apply_it: Do one small, physical thing for your local environment today, such as planting, picking up litter or watering a tree.

quiz.question: How did the Green Belt Movement help women beyond planting trees?
options: It gave them income, confidence and a public voice
It replaced their farms with factories
It had no effect on women
quiz.explanation: Paying women for surviving seedlings brought income and skills, and the movement helped women take part in public life.

cards.title: Polish shipyard workers built a union that outlasted martial law
cards.body:
In August 1980, workers at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk, Poland, went on strike after a popular crane operator, Anna Walentynowicz, was fired. An unemployed electrician, Lech Walesa, climbed the shipyard wall to help lead them.

The strike spread, and within weeks the communist government agreed to allow an independent trade union: Solidarity. Around ten million people joined, roughly a third of Poland's working-age population.

In December 1981 the government declared martial law, banned Solidarity and jailed thousands. The movement went underground, printing newsletters and keeping in touch. In 1989, with the economy failing, the government sat down to talk. In partly free elections that June, Solidarity won nearly every seat it was allowed to contest.

A movement can be banned and still win, if its people stay connected.
cards.apply_it: Reconnect with one person who shares a goal or value with you, even with a short message.

quiz.question: What happened to Solidarity after martial law in 1981?
options: It went underground and later won elections in 1989
quiz.explanation: Banned and persecuted, Solidarity kept going in secret and won a sweeping victory in Poland's partly free 1989 elections.

cards.title: Peaceful crowds, not armies, opened the Berlin Wall
cards.body:
For 28 years the Berlin Wall split a city and symbolised the Cold War. In autumn 1989, East Germans began gathering after Monday prayers in Leipzig churches. On 9 October around 70,000 people marched carrying candles, chanting that they were the people. Security forces were ready to shoot, but faced with such numbers and such calm, they did not.

On 9 November, a government spokesman fumbled a press conference and suggested new travel rules took effect immediately. Thousands of East Berliners rushed to the checkpoints. Late that night, at one crossing, an overwhelmed officer opened the gate. Crowds poured through, climbing and chipping at the Wall in celebration.

No single leader planned it. Ordinary people, simply showing up in large and peaceful numbers, made the old order impossible to keep.
cards.apply_it: Show up for one community event, meeting or vigil this month; presence itself matters.

quiz.question: What opened the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989?
options: Crowds of East Berliners at the checkpoints after a confused announcement
A secret treaty signed years earlier
quiz.explanation: After an official's muddled announcement, huge peaceful crowds gathered at the checkpoints until guards opened the gates.

cards.title: Whistle-blowers show that one honest insider can expose a lie
cards.body:
Sometimes change starts with a single person who sees wrongdoing from the inside and refuses to stay quiet.

In 1971 Daniel Ellsberg, a military analyst, leaked a secret study showing that US leaders had misled the public about the Vietnam War. The US Supreme Court allowed newspapers to publish it. In 2001 Sherron Watkins, an accountant at the energy firm Enron, warned her boss in writing about hidden losses shortly before the company collapsed.

Whistle-blowing can cost people their careers, friendships and peace of mind, so it pays to do it wisely. Keep careful records, raise concerns through proper channels or an official regulator where possible, and get independent advice. Many countries now have laws, such as the UK's Public Interest Disclosure Act, that protect workers who speak up responsibly.
cards.apply_it: Find out who you would report serious wrongdoing to at your workplace or school, and note it down.

quiz.question: Which is a wise step for someone thinking of blowing the whistle?
options: Keep records and seek independent advice
quiz.explanation: Careful records, proper channels and independent advice help whistle-blowers be heard and protected.

cards.title: Apartheid ended after decades of pressure from millions of people
cards.body:
Nelson Mandela is the face of South Africa's freedom, but he spent 27 years in prison while others kept the struggle alive.

On 16 June 1976, thousands of schoolchildren in Soweto marched against being forced to learn in Afrikaans. Police opened fire, and the killings drew the world's attention. In 1983, hundreds of community, church, student and workers' groups joined together as the United Democratic Front. People organised rent strikes, consumer boycotts and labour strikes.

Abroad, ordinary people refused to buy South African goods, pressed universities to sell investments and supported sports boycotts. Under this pressure the government released Mandela in 1990. In April 1994, millions of South Africans queued for hours to vote in the first elections open to all races.

Leaders matter, but movements carry them.
cards.apply_it: Look up the story behind one product or company you use, and decide whether you are comfortable supporting it.

quiz.question: What role did schoolchildren play in the fight against apartheid?
options: They ended apartheid alone in one day
Soweto students marched in 1976, drawing world attention
quiz.explanation: The 1976 Soweto student protest and the brutal response turned global attention to apartheid and energised resistance.

cards.title: Courage, organising and persistence are skills anyone can build
cards.body:
Look back at these stories and the same lessons appear.

Courage is contagious. One person's stand gives others permission to act, but it works best when backed by preparation. Organising wins. Carpools, leaflets, underground newsletters and coalitions turned anger into lasting power. Persistence matters, because most victories took decades, not days.

Nonviolence has a strong record. Researchers who studied hundreds of campaigns from 1900 to 2006 found nonviolent ones succeeded about twice as often as violent ones, partly because more people can join them.

Finally, small acts add up: a seat, a seedling, a handful of salt, a candle. You do not need to be famous or powerful. You need to notice what is wrong, find others who care, and take the next small step, again and again.
cards.apply_it: Choose one small act for the cause you named at the start of this guide, and do it before the week ends.

quiz.question: Why have nonviolent campaigns succeeded about twice as often as violent ones?
options: Partly because many more people can take part in them
quiz.explanation: Nonviolent movements tend to draw much wider participation, which gives them more power and legitimacy.
